utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, you asked for further guidance as to the time still available for the examination-in-chief of Mr. Krajisnik. We hope to give that to you later this afternoon, and if we do not manage to do that it will not be later than Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I'll remind you that you're bound -- still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I'll invite Mr. Josse to continue his examination-in-chief. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I deal with one practical matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that Mr. Krajisnik has brought to the Chamber this morning various documents. I think they're documents that involve Mr. Davidovic. He's provided five copies; they're with the registrar at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm not clear about is whether those are the documents that need to go to me first of all to assess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- if there are any documents given to the registrar, I'd like to see them so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there's apparently a CD. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a CD which, from what I see, contains copies of documents and -- if you would just give me a minute to have a look at them. It's -- I'm just trying to -- to see what we are talking about. First of all I see a few -- copies of a few pages of Mr. Owen's book, Balkan Odyssey, and what I see is that it very much gives me the impression that these are the same pages but we have a B/C/S copy and a -- different, of course, in numbering, but the same pages in B/C/S and in English. Then we have a copy with some underlining in the text of page 178 of a book which at least bears the word "catastrophe" in its title. In B/C/S only, not any English translation. Then we have -- it gives me the impression that it would be something coming from Bijeljina, something that -- what seems to be, at first sight -- well, let's say another document from the north-East Bosnia. I see another -- what seems to be a decision of the 18th of November, 1994, which is far beyond -- and which seems to be a decision from Bijeljina. Then we have another document, 4th of July, 1995, from Bijeljina as well; and then a document from the 4th of September, 1993; and one document which is -- it mainly is about Bijeljina. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, is it more or less right what I said about what kind of documents we have in front of us? And could you tell us what's on the CD-ROM. Is that copies of the same documents or are they different matters on the CD-ROM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On CD-ROM there are all documents but one plus all the statements of certain witnesses concerning Davidovic. All this concerns Davidovic and one protected witness we mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it your wish that they'll be given to Mr. Josse in order for him to have a look at them and see whether they could be of any use for the examination-in-chief for the times to come or -- is that what you intend to do -- what you wish me to do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said yesterday that if I have any documents concerning Mr. Davidovic I should bring them today. I brought five copies for everybody. Those are Davidovic documents, and this supplement here concerning Mr. Owen and Mr. Zimmermann is related to the protected witness. I wanted to tell you today what I intended to produce to Mr. Davidovic back at that time. If the Defence does not have these documents, I can give them those concerning Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you noticed- and I informed Mr. Josse yesterday on the relevant passages of the testimony of Mr. Davidovic. I pointed at the pages, the date at least, and what more or less happened ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we'll give them to Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse is -- if he was not yesterday, then certainly today he's fully aware of all the procedural aspects involved. He'll give it some thought on whether he sees -- because it's clear now that it would be your wish to have them brought to the attention of the Chamber. He will, from his professional point of view, he'll certainly see whether there's any -- any way of introducing these documents into evidence. And then Mr. Josse will address the Chamber on the matter if he sees any possibility to do so. If not, then at the end of your testimony -- of course, you're free again to talk to Mr. Josse and you would have an opportunity to discuss further with him whether at that moment, apart from whether it would need any recall of Mr. Krajisnik as a witness, whether there would be any possibility to have them introduced into evidence, unless the Prosecution would have any objection against handing out these documents at this moment to Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, would you please pass this to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have all five sets, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, saves you the copying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are other reasons as well. It's not for us to look at unless you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. If this is the procedure, then I would like to have your permission to add something to my yesterday's testimony regarding those witnesses. I can add it as a summary. It's in response to the questions of Mr. Josse concerning Mr. Davidovic and the protected witness. I just want to point something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you say at this moment, since you have no direct possibility of introducing these documents, that you would like to add to your answers given yesterday. Mr. Krajisnik, I explain one thing for you. Of course the Chamber, without even knowing what they are and aware of all the problems that we could expect if we now introduce in a -- in an informal way and not in accordance with Rule 92 bis any of these statements, of course the Chamber could decide that they could be admitted, but there -- first of all, the Chamber would, from a procedural point of view, not be surprised if an objection would come - and I see Mr. Harmon nodding "yes." That's one. So it would need certainly more, I would say, procedural debate before we could take such a decision. But there's also another matter involved. Mr. Josse, your Defence counsel, are under a duty to look after carefully your interest. The Chamber, by not knowing what is in these documents, by deciding that they could be admitted could admit documents which, apart from the points you wanted to draw our attention to, could admit material which might not in every respect be favourable. And it's finally up to Defence counsel - perhaps together with you but communication is difficult at this moment - it's for Defence counsel to assess whether any such risks do exist. They may well not be there, but it's proper to give an opportunity to Defence counsel before we even start the procedural debate to see whether it would, on the balance of what you seek and what they might perceive as risks, to consider whether we should enter in such a debate at all. Mr. Josse, is that more or less what you would have put to Mr. Krajisnik if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I'm not arguing with a word that Your Honour has said. Having said that, I would invite Mr. Krajisnik to add any supplementary remarks that he might have, which is a -- which may be a slightly different issue to the one that Your Honour has just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not commenting on that; I was just commenting on why the Chamber at this moment remitted the documents to you and did not -- just without full knowledge say: Well, we accept these documents, apart from the procedural debate that would be necessary anyhow, but also for the other reasons why we could not at this moment even start such a debate. But of course this would not prevent you in any way inviting Mr. Krajisnik to add to his answers he gave yesterday. May I then take it this would be your first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, two things. First of all, I'm going to ask you to add anything you want in relation to Mr. Davidovic; therefore, I'm going to invite the Chamber to go into private session in any event. So let's deal with it in that manner. Do bear in mind what the learned Judge told you today and yesterday. What you can't do is simply tell the Chamber what is contained within statements that have been obtained on your behalf by investigators or other people. But go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best to abide by those guidelines. Yesterday I was asked to comment on the statement of Mr. Davidovic that he had seen a document I signed not in 1992. Although it was not in 1992, he saw the document in the hands of Mr. Vojislav [as interpreted] Djurkovic. He did not see the date on the document, but he allegedly saw the signature of Momcilo Krajisnik. I can say that concerning exchanges of civilians or prisoners of war, Mr. Vojkan Djurkovic was in charge, and it is necessary to establish, in my opinion, evidence as to when he took over that job; in other words, to establish whether the document itself originates from 1992, 1993, or 1994. I assert before this Court that Witness Vojislav Djurkovic, to the best of my knowledge, could only have taken that post overseeing exchanges of prisoners in July 1993. And any document related to those affairs could only be from that date or later. And it was my intention to prove this through the documents I have produced. There's another thing I want to point out regarding Mr. Davidovic. It is a great pity - and Mr. Josse did not ask me this - that some other incriminating things he mentioned have not been checked, like that I took money from the customs to Pale. I said yesterday that I didn't take any money at all, I didn't carry any money ever. But this is a specific case, and some sort of receipt should be found from that institution to prove this. You can only take my word for it, and I'm saying that I didn't, but unfortunately there is no document to prove this. The customs office keeps documents for three years or so. Second, he stated that he had been at Mount Jahorina providing security to the government in the month of April and early May. I wish to point out -- I hope I did not digress from the subject. I wish to point out that this is not true because the government went to Jahorina only in end May and early June, and we were able to see that from statements that speak to the contrary of that assertion of that witness. You also questioned me yesterday about the seizure of vehicles that were confiscated. You asked me if I had any knowledge about this. There is evidence - and I found one case by chance - that one vehicle was indeed seized and the document was signed by Mr. Davidovic as signing that vehicle to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I managed to find out, and I said yesterday that such things did occur during the war. Another thing I wanted to say is that we have a trial here but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Davidovic said, for reasons I cannot begin to understand, that Mr. Karadzic and I quarrelled very badly about the distribution of money, about the division of money, in New York. Initially he said New York in 1992 and then in Geneva or I don't know where. I tried to find evidence about this, although he didn't even mention who exactly was involved, and I wasn't able to establish who was in our group at the time or anything else. All I can say is that this is complete fabrication. Another thing. I was asked yesterday to try to guess the motivation of Mr. Davidovic for lying, if I think he's lying. He sounded very convincing, and I tried to think of what could have possibly motivated him. I could only think of the fact that he was in the communist party and I wasn't; that's one reason. Another thing. There are documents to prove that he was decorated for his participation before the war in Kosovo as a member of a special unit. He could also have seen the SDS as the main culprit, and he testified against me possibly because of the abundance of disinformation that circulated. And he may have seen me as the main culprit, the representative of that SDS that replaced him from his post of chief of police. Third, when he was in the federal MUP, he used to sign documents as chief of police of Bijeljina. He did not actually occupy that post, which goes to show that he did certain things of his own accord, arbitrarily. It is also my impression that the man is obviously a brave policeman who had his place in a former system, and nowadays, being very disappointed, he put all this disinformation together to incriminate me. And lastly, I wish to emphasise that I don't know the man, nor did I ever sit down together with him. And in conclusion let me say that I can provide documents to prove all the things that I say -- that I said that I wasn't at Pale, that he signed certain papers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The papers that you say he has signed, is that in the bundle that you provided this morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it was my intention to provide copies for everyone in the courtroom but my lawyer has taken them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I like paper, Mr. Krajisnik. We will return to this subject sometime next week, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, about this second witness, the protected one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You may proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go back and deal with a few more intercepts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik have the bundle of intercepts -- he has his own, I beg your pardon, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the one, then that's it, the one I've got. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going to tell us which number on the list, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it's 188 in the left-hand margin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is P292 KID31425, also P389 KID31425. It's a -- it's a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and a Mr. Mijatovic, and then later on between Mr. Krajisnik and a Mr. Vladusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before we look at the conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, or bits of because it's quite long, who is Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic was the president of the Executive Board of the Rajlovac municipality and my kum. That is to say my father was godfather to his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Mr. Vladusic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vladusic was a distant relevant. His mother and my father were brother and sister, so he's a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this intercept was played to this Court on the 2nd of November of 2004 at page 7833 of the transcript during the evidence of a man called Elvir Jahic. There was a very lengthy, or relatively lengthy, legal argument as to whether the witness was in a position to say that this intercept was in some way proof that you knew about the detention of men in the system close to Ahatovici. For what it's worth, it's not entirely clear to me whether the witness did in fact say that. However, it's clearly the Prosecution case that this intercept is evidence or gives rise to an inference that you did have that knowledge. In particular there are two passages that, as I understand it, the Prosecution rely upon. On page 2 in the English, you say to Mr. Mijatovic: "Because they have released some men. They went from here. They are back again. Yes, yes, so they are attacking, aren't they?" Mijatovic: "Yes, that's it." Krajisnik: "Well, you see it. You are a smart man, so that ..." Mijatovic: "You know, you know what -- why is this part now to say so separated military and civilian. Krajisnik: "Yes." Mijatovic: "Well, here I think we -- these women, they're accommodated I think ... As many as was possible ... Women, children, and old men with certain conditions. And the military part, that is for the military police, and that part there will be processed and so on. They are investigating, completing it, and now what are they going to process. Believe me that I don't know." Now, this is going to be a rather long question, but I'd now like to turn to page 4 in the English, and I am going to ask you, Mr. Krajisnik -- I am going to tell you the place in your language in a moment. I am going to ask you to read a bit of in slowly because we, perhaps, have some translation issues. The passage I'd like you to read from is on the 5th page in the B/C/S, and it is very near the top of the page that begins "nema toga." I'd like to read what you say there, then what Mr. Vladusic says, then what you and he say thereafter. Read it slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference in English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In English it's page 4, but I would invite the interpreters to try and, of course, interpret what the witness is saying rather than what's written down in English. The purpose of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, at the same time it would be good if they can see how it was translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so they can compare and see whether they identify any portion of which might need a review.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Krajisnik, if you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've understood that you want me to read that part of the text. Krajisnik, that's me: "There's no one who should now ... Innocent people, because they're Muslims, because somebody has provided them with weapons, if they've done nothing, if they've surrendered, from Gacanovici, you know, thank God, what's over there." And then Ljubisa Vladusic says: "Wait. Can you influence the situation in any way?" Krajisnik: "Yes, I can, and I told that soldiers. Nobody must do anything. They are now -- yes, I understand doing ... Nobody must do anything that's not proper, whether it be a Muslim, nobody should kill him. Heaven forbid." Vladusic: "I discussed that with Mirko, and I'm very pleased to see that he thinks the same way, and you have an identical opinion and I'm very happy to hear that. Because I thought that, that involved that there was a lot involved with all that." Krajisnik: "No way."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make this observation. Your Honour might recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just let me re-read and compare the translation as we receive it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When this evidence was originally given, Your Honour spent some time, very helpfully, clarifying with Mr. Jahic that the reference to Gacanovic was, in fact, Gacanovici. That was of course clarified during the Prosecution case and that Gacanovici, what Mr. Jahic meant, was a large family as well as some reference to a village. So that part had been previously clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, those two passages, that is the one on page 4 in the English and the one at the very beginning on page 2, that -- as I've already said, the Prosecution assert gives rise to an inference that you knew about what was going on in the cisterns. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew - and from this conversation you can see that and probably before that as well - that a certain number of Muslims had been taken prisoner from the village of Ahatovici, which is the neighbouring village in the Rajlovac region, in the Rajlovac garrison, in the cisterns or whatever, so I knew about that. Now, this is a conversation that is linked to that previous knowledge of mine, however what is actually happening over there, that's another matter, I can explain that. But that I knew they can be captured? Yes, I did, I knew that, and it's in my municipality; that's what I want to stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand the reason for their detention to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that proceedings were under -- or rather, that there was fighting in Dobrosevici when the Serbs and the Ahatovici people. And then the Territorial Defence took them prisoner and took them off towards the Rajlovac garrison. I knew nothing about that before, and now, as prisoners -- they were there as prisoners. And then the people followed them, and here they say that the women and children were separated and accommodated as far as was possible, whereas the military-able men were being interrogated by the soldiers, that is to say by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand the nature of their detention to be? Let me explain that. Where were they being held? What conditions? So on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember whether I knew -- that I knew where they were put up, where they were detained, because I see here that they were detained in a number of locations. But I did know that they were somewhere in Rajlovac, that was something I did know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Specifically in the passage that you have just read you say, and I'm reading now from today's translation: "Yes, I can, and I told that soldiers nobody must do anything." What did you mean when you said: "And I told that soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might I say something before I answer? Traditionally, the Muslims and Serbs, in all wars in that region, and especially the Muslims from Ahatovici -- we're talking about the Gacanovici family. Anyway, the Mujkics and others. They were -- had very close relations and ties, and the Serbs and the Muslims got on very well, looking out for each other. My mother comes from that region, and she told -- often told me how during World War II Serb girls -- the Muslims put Muslim clothes, traditional clothes, on Serb girls and hid them away when the Ustashas came by -- Ustashas were Muslims, too, there were Muslim Ustashas as well - in order to save them from a terrible fate. And so, for a long time my brother and I felt gratitude towards those people who had saved these girls. And I went to school with the Gacanovici children, primary school and secondary school. So this wasn't an all-out conflict; it was a conflict in which I, from Pale, saw no reason for anybody to be harmed, not a hair on their head should be harmed. And as we're talking about my municipality, my brother informed me that a certain number of Muslims had been detained in Rajlovac - I was in Pale myself - and he told me the names, he mentioned the family names of these people. And then here in this particular conversation I confirm and say that I talked to some of the soldiers or one of the soldiers and said everything I said, that they should not be allowed to do something that is not all right. Not as somebody issuing orders, but because I'd like to draw their attention to the fact that I have a particular interest in this event and I see no reason why anybody should suffer because -- for the mere fact of being a Muslim, if he gave weapons, if he had surrendered weapons. And I said that they had come from this other municipality. The group of Muslims from Bratunac were exchanged via Ilijas and went to Visoko and some of them were taken prisoner in Ahatovici. And I said at the time that if someone gives up weapons you can't kill them. The people were released from Pale, so there shouldn't be any retaliation. Now, why was I afraid of retaliation and revenge? Because in this barracks you had a large number of refugees who had collected there. Their families had been killed. From Popovici [phoen], for example, their houses had been destroyed. So they weren't locals, they weren't the local population who know Ahatovici very well, but people who thought they should take their revenge against someone. That's what I was afraid of, and that's why I said that care and attention should be paid that this doesn't happen. And here I was talking to civilians and people close to me, the civilian authorities, and I wanted to tell them what I thought about the matter. We all thought the same, but they were just cautioning me and saying that these military-able men came under the authority of the army. So the sense of all this, what this means, I was a little rhetorical perhaps, it wouldn't have been something that the Serb people would be prone to do, to do something improper, to kill a blameless man for the mere fact that that person had a weapon in his hands. So that is what I mean when I said this here during this information. Unfortunately some people did lose their lives, others were exchanged, but that's another matter, whereas here I took this position, I took this view, and you can see that this other man Mr. Vladusic says: "Well, I'm very happy that you think the same way as I do." And Mijatovic thought the same way, too, thought the same thing. But it was the Rajlovac garrison that was in charge, the military unit and so on. I don't know who I talked to. Perhaps I talked to a commander or that commander. I don't know what the man was, but it was a man talking, that is to say I was saying that I don't want anything improper to take place in my municipality because that would reflect badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other question about this intercept. A few lines further down, same page I think in both languages, you say: "One cannot engage in genocide to achieve anything. I know that it is difficult when someone is killed." Now, to some extent, you have just explained that remark in the long answer that you have given. But what did you mean and why did you choose the word "genocide"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- at that time I didn't know I would end up in The Hague Tribunal. In our parts of the world when you are trying to get a serious point across, you tend to use the heaviest qualification because whatever lighter words you use, the other person tends to take it lightly. When you say "genocide" -- when I said "genocide," I mean that nobody had a right to take revenge. I wasn't thinking of the legal qualification of genocide; I was talking in more traditional terms, like you don't kill a person who has his hands tied. It's our tradition, you have the right to try them or something else, although maybe not in war, but you don't have the right to kill them. That's how I saw things and that was the opinion of every honourable person. And in one conversation here there is a reference to another event. We attended a funeral of a member of the Moro family who was killed by a sniper while on guard, and that inflamed passions. And I said: Nobody has the right to take revenge. I knew the man personally; he was a wonderful person, this Moro man. He was killed by a sniper while on guard. He was standing on the defence line as a member of the Territorial Defence, and I meant also those people who came from outside because civilians and refugees all tended to flow into the barracks. It was all overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next intercept, please, 190 in the left-hand margin. This is a longish conversation between you and your brother. It's P282 and P292 KID31460 and P369. It has been --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Krajisnik. It's -- was referred to initially in this Court on the 21st of September, 2004, during the evidence of 623 and was then played to this Court on the 28th of September, the same year, at 6217 in the transcript during the evidence of Mr. Kljujic. There are a number of different points in this I want to ask you about, and then I'll perhaps turn to what Mr. Kljujic had to say about it. On page 2 in the English you are asking your brother: "What's going on?" And he says: "I don't know what to tell you. Some shooting started just now." You ask: "Where?" He says: "Cannons around the village." What's he referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says that shooting is targeting Zabrdje. I must have called him up while he was at home. He couldn't have been at the barracks. He could have been only at our home in Zabrdje, and the cannons were firing from the Muslim side by night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we go to the third page in English, we see -- you say: "He called me from Izetbegovic's office to check but in front." Mirko: "Where did he inform? He asked of you not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper up there. His mother has been wounded and things like that." Momcilo: "Not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper." Mirko: "Yeah." And eventually Mirko says: "Vito called me." It was that part of the evidence 623 commented about, as did Mr. Kljujic. Tell the Chamber what you understand the discussion about the JAT skyscraper to involve.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see a reference here to the name Karkin. Fahrija Karkin was a lawyer from Sarajevo. At some point in 1980-something, he was on my defence team in the lawsuit that the Trial Chamber is familiar with. I remained on good terms with him. Just to illustrate, I wanted him to be on my Defence team here in The Hague, and he visited me once. But for some reason he was not able to be part of my team. Apparently, from this conversation, he called my brother from the office of Mr. Izetbegovic. Let me explain why he called. His idea was to get me and Mr. Izetbegovic together in order to revive an initiative so that the two of us should talk. He didn't call back; I don't know why. But when he said to my brother: Tell him not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper. In Sarajevo in the 1960s, the first skyscraper was built in the eastern part of Sarajevo and all the skyscrapers built later were not referred to as skyscrapers. This is the only building called a skyscraper in the old part of town. And since it held the branch of the Yugoslav airlines, JAT, from Belgrade, it was commonly referred to as the JAT skyscraper, otherwise it was a residential building and his mother happened to live there. When he said what he said, he didn't mean that I am the one who was shooting or that I could stop anything. His mother was ill or injured, and he was trying to convey to me, as his friend or acquaintance, that he doesn't want shooting to target that building. He's letting me know about his personal problem, although that has nothing to do with me or any kind of command nor could I have given any orders one way or another, nor was anybody targeting the skyscraper, but it was probably somebody doing something inappropriate. As for this person Vito, it was Vitomir Zepinic calling from Sarajevo. This person has been mentioned here. After the war started, he stayed there. At one point he wanted to get out of Sarajevo and he did get out, travelling in the boot of a passenger car because he couldn't take it any longer in Sarajevo. He lives in Australia today. That was the passage that you have read so far, and those are my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the next page there's a discussion about Mr. Kecmanovic's position within the Presidency and Mr. Pelivan's appointment as Prime Minister. I'm, in fact, not going to ask you about that. What I would like to do is turn the page to 5 -- unless you're anxious to comment on that, Mr. Krajisnik. Perhaps you are.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps I can give a brief comment, it would be useful. Mr. Pejanovic was frequently in touch with my brother during the war, seeking contacts with me, and that's how we kept in touch, through my brother. He would call up Mirko, Mirko would call up me. And here again he has some information apparently about the Presidency that he could have received from my brother, but also from Zepinic. So we see from here that I'm interested in what's going on in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, and I'm also interested in any indications that could point to a change in policy and the likelihood of a solution. That brings me to the testimony of Mr. Kecmanovic, who testified here. He said that although a consensus had been expected, Pejanovic and Kecmanovic entered the Presidency on the understanding that a consensus would exist on all -- that all decisions of the Presidency would be taken by consensus. And Mr. Kecmanovic wants to replace him now because something was done about the appointment of Mr. Pelivan without consensus. That is another piece of background that can help understand the testimony of Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So turning the page to page 5 in the English at the bottom, I'm going to read out a passage. Your brother says: "Fuck. This morning I heard the Muslims who were running away from Misoca" -- perhaps you can pronounce that for me -- "killed a full bus of Serbs in Srednji. Misoca was being cleansed. Yeah. So Muslims killed a full bus of Serbs." You say: "How? "Your brother, who were on their way to Pale as refugees, just a little while ago they told me this wasn't the case but in fact they took these prisoners with them. Actually, an older sergeant who does exchanges up there received a phone call from the city. Can you hear me? Momcilo say it again." Mirko: "This guy from the city called me. You know. But what was his name? Alispahic and he said those prisoners had been killed." Momcilo: "What prisoners? Mirko: "They took the prisoners to Pale again." A number of questions arise from this passage. Firstly, and perhaps most importantly of all, Mr. Kljujic was asked about ethnic cleansing from Misoca and a reference to this passage was made, in particular the words: "Misoca was being cleansed." Help the Trial Chamber with that, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was said just by the way in this conversation; it was not the subject of our conversation. I am not an expert who would be qualified to explain what cleansing means, but I heard experts talk about it. Cleansing meant mopping-up, driving out the enemy; it never meant cleansing the population. If by coincidence the population left as well, there were such cases, but that's another matter. Whenever mopping-up was mentioned or clearing the field or things like that, that meant driving out the enemy. It doesn't mean that we were cleansing civilians. It doesn't mean, either, that in some cases civilians didn't leave as well, but in this specific case Muslims and Serbs battled in the Ilijas municipality, and when the battle was over mopping-up began to mop-up the pockets of resistance, to drive out the enemy that still remained in the area. That is the explanation I heard from military people on both sides; mopping-up, clearing, means clearing the field from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thereafter your brother informs you that the Muslims killed a full bus of Serbs. At that point did you have any knowledge of that attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. But if I may suggest to the esteemed Trial Chamber, it would be good to have a map in front of us to show you where it happened. It happened in no-man's land. Maybe then you would get a different picture. To get there you have to cross a mountain, and this happened in no-man's land. It would be easier to explain with a map. I didn't know - and you can see from this intercept that I didn't know about it - and I was greatly surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll organise that for about the break, but let's -- a bit of groundwork before we get there. First of all, what attack is he actually referring to? Let's not worry about the location of the attack. Tell us about the attack and what you subsequently learned about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt then from my brother that prisoners from Rajlovac had been taken to Pale by this roundabout route, the other roundabout route via Visojevica after the slaughter in Misoca, which was on the separation line. Because the people on the bus with were thought to be Serbs because they were travelling on a Serb bus. Mr. Alispahic promised to get revenge because he accused people from Rajlovac, although it was a hundred kilometres away. Some prisoners had been exchanged, but this busload of people had not been exchanged. They tried one or two different routes and ended up slaughtered in that spot. We have heard one witness who testified about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you've just referred to the slaughter in Misoca. What slaughter are you referring to there and who was slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say slaughter in Misoca. I said that there was probably a clash between Muslims and Serbs, and I see from this text that Muslims who had escaped from there - it's very close by - they, according to the first information, thinking that it was a Serb bus, fired at the bus and shot those people dead. That's what I said. And they killed, actually, prisoners who were travelling to be exchanged on that bus. That's what I see from here and that's what I learnt then, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. This needs some clarification, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, what ethnicity, in fact, were the people in the bus?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those same Muslim prisoners who had been detained in Rajlovac; that's one group of them. And another group had previously been exchanged. In other words, Muslims from Ahatovici, a certain number of them was put on a bus to take them to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you've explained this but I'm going to ask you again. At this point in time, why did your brother believe that the occupants of the bus were Serbs, when in fact they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He received reports by radio or something -- you see he says here: "I was informed this morning that this happened." Somebody told him. He's just passing on what he heard from somebody, he's passing it on to me. You see further up where he says: "I heard this morning that a busload of Muslims were killed. Muslims thought they were Serbs." So he's passing on what he heard from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the answer you gave earlier you used the word "slaughter." There's clearly some confusion about that. Who did you say had been slaughtered? In what context did you use this word in relation to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain I did not use the word "slaughter." I said: The people on the bus were killed. Maybe that's an error. "Slaughter" is a totally different term in the Serbian language. So Muslim prisoners were killed, prisoners that were being driven by bus towards Pale using the only available route at the time, a roundabout route, going through Vogosca, Ilijas, and so on. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue. Yes, yes, I said "killed numbers, large numbers." I said that. The interpreters have just given me the word I used precisely. I thank them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the intercept goes on, and if you need the map to answer this question say so and we'll deal with this immediately after the break. The point I left off was your brother says: "They took the prisoners to Pale again." You say: "Yes." And he says: "At Srednji they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all those prisoners. Our two men have been heavily wounded." You said: "They thought those were our people." "They thought those were our people," says your brother. Is that the same instance that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the same incident. He is just conveying to me the information he received from the Serb side because those two wounded had been brought in. I don't know whether there were two wounded men, but there must have been because otherwise he wouldn't be telling me that. So somebody said this to my brother and he's passing it on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then finally your brother goes on: "Tonight they want to retaliate against all Serbs in the city and in prison." You say: "Yeah." He says: "To kill them all." You say: "Unbelievable." And he says: "Supposedly they will use their cutthroats to attack Rajlovac in groups and all kinds of things like that." Was this some sort of fanciful conversation that you were having with your brother, or was this your genuine belief at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on your question, but I'll do my best to answer because I know what my brother actually said. He was also conveying a conversation -- the conversation of someone talking to Mr. Alispahic, and my brother also had contacts with him later, a telephone conversation, because they knew each other, we were neighbours. And this man said - I assume, I can only assume - that Alispahic said: You killed the Muslims, now we're going to kill all the Serbs in town and we're going to take our revenge. And there's an expression that we say, perhaps coming from the Turkish language, the person that killed with the guillotine, the henchman, and that he would take his revenge from Rajlovac. I don't know whether that actually took place, whether they attacked Rajlovac or not. But Mr. Alispahic, even if he said that, probably had reason to be angry because a large number of people close to him were killed. Now, I'm not justifying him, but especially as the day before he managed to exchange his family at Bozici pump -- petrol station. And these other people stayed on and criticised him for having exchanged his own family, where others were killed. I can't remember which this Alispahic person was, although I know the Alispahic family. So if he did say that, he said that in a state of revolt, indignation. Why? Because on the Muslim side somebody said the Serbs killed them, just as somebody had told my brother: Well, it was the Muslims who killed them. So when you receive information like that to the effect that some people were killed by others and you wanted to have them exchanged, your reaction in wartime is normal, the kind that Mr. Alispahic had, on the other side of course, because we're not dealing with animals, we're dealing with living people and one's neighbours. So I understand that type of rhetoric, so he was probably angry. And I don't believe that they retaliated against the Serbs in Sarajevo in that connection. That was done systematically by gangs that were rampant in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a convenient moment to have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For a few procedural issues, I'd first like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more matters, procedural matters. The Chamber will now deal with some exhibits which are ready to be admitted. Exhibit 1081 is an English transcript of an interview of Mr. Poplasen. On the 5th of May the Prosecution explained that this document was identical to P1081.1, which is already in evidence. The Defence has requested some time to review these documents and was granted one week. Reference is made to transcript page 23625. No objections have been raised, therefore P1081 is admitted into evidence. On the 11th of May, the Prosecution submitted the following video clips on a CD: P1083, P1088, P1089, P1090, and P1091. These were video clips which were played during the testimony of Mr. Poplasen. The Defence was given one week to raise objections, transcript page 23863. No objections have been raised, and therefore these exhibits are admitted into evidence. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am -- I'm not going to be very much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, have a look at this map, and perhaps you can tell the Court if this is going to assist in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would even assist if the Chamber would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I've got lots of copies of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Or if it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But frankly, all I wanted to do at this stage is find out if it's the right map. If it's not, I'm going to sit down and Mr. Stewart is going to take over and I'm going to try to get the right map during the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does that map do the trick? If it doesn't, say so, and we'll try again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The trick?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In relation to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something lacking here, part of the map towards Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought that was the case; that's why I asked the question. I'm going to sit down. Mr. Stewart's going to take over. I'm going to try to get a better map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And even from what I remember it happened close to Vogosca going around, and especially that portion is not missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly I thought that. I thought that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll return the maps to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Logistical problems, photocopiers are not working, some real assistance from the Prosecution I must say, however, and I'm grateful for that. We'll try again. Perhaps I could return to this subject after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to drive the Defence bus for a while now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- What I want us to go to is a series in what I will call a neutral broad descriptive way, a series of Presidency meetings and minutes and then from time to time government minutes, and we're talking about the period May and June 1992. Somebody's microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've no idea. Somebody's microphone is by a lot of papers. It seems to have -- that seems to have resolved itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, could we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And could Mr. Krajisnik be given this material? It's the minutes of the Presidency of the Serbian republic held on the 12th of May, 1992, P64A, binder 22, tab 613. It's also P65, binder 12, tab 144. Your Honour, we've notified - and I hope that's got through all right - a list of a number of items of this nature that we'll be coming to fairly soon. So I hope from a practical point of view that there is a programme of documents to be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I'm not sure Mr. Krajisnik's got the document yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what you're about to be given is minutes of what's described in English of the first constitutive session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 12th of May, 1992. We're just waiting for you to be able to have that in your own language. There seem to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can, I think, offer a solution to this. There seems to be a hitch that, unlike the normal position for various practical reasons, this material is not readily available in court. Your Honour, we can't solve the immediate problem on this item unless Mr. Krajisnik has it, but what I can do, Your Honour, is make sure over the next few minutes we can get print-outs of the B/C/S versions of all the items I'm going to be referring to so that we have a batch in court for Mr. Krajisnik. I can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we proceed having it put on the ELMO for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We -- it should be very quick, knowing Mr. Sladojevic's work. We'll just get all those items ready for Mr. Krajisnik and as long as it takes to just get them printed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I take it you've put away some files of your own. This is a fairly short item anyway, Mr. Krajisnik, so I'll read the short item from the English. "On the 12th of May, 1992, after the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina elected Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, and Dr. Nikola Koljevic as members of the Presidency, the Presidency held its first constitutive session. In addition to the members of the Presidency, the session was attended by Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the Assembly; and Dr. Branko Djeric, the Prime Minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the items on the agenda was the election of the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Members of the president" -- sorry. "Member," singular, "of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic was unanimously elected the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Krajisnik, so far as the content of that minute is concerned, one never knows -- there appears to be nothing controversial in any of those items, but are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what -- first of all, can you say who was there at that meeting, which was the first -- apparently the first Presidency meeting after that Banja Luka Assembly meeting and on the same day, apparently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting the same day, but there's something illogical here that was that Mrs. Plavsic wasn't there, didn't attend that meeting, and I can explain how the decision was taken unanimously, if you're interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please do explain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that two members of the Presidency, Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, wanted responsibility for this most important role to be vested in Mr. Karadzic, as long as the constitution was being amended. And before that, they agreed it would be a good idea to choose a three-member Presidency with him as the president. It's probable that Mrs. Plavsic was contacted, either by telephone or when she first returned to Pale. In any case, they had her approval. So this document records that it was a unanimous decision, although Mrs. Plavsic was not at Pale. I don't remember it exactly, but I think that it was announced during a break that Mr. Karadzic would be the president of the Presidency. And even before the session it was a matter that was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was taking minutes of -- who took minutes of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know, but it stands to reason that it was written later because we see the signature of Mrs. Plavsic. So she must have signed later, not on the 12th of May. Some assistant wrote this down. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, there were, we can see, between this date, the 12th of May and the next Presidency meeting for which we have a minute, there were then a -- which was the 31st of May, there were several government meetings. First of all, can you say whether you personally attended any sessions or meetings of the government with or without the National Security Council between that meeting and the Assembly session on the 12th of May and the next meeting of the Presidency on the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment the government was established, which was the 12th of May, it started its completely autonomous work, and there were no expanded meetings anymore where non-government members would be included. And I don't remember attending any one of them, apart from a break in the Assembly session in Bijeljina. That was the only occasion when I was present, but I didn't attend a single official meeting of the government because the government worked independently, which stands to reason. We are talking about government sessions, right, cabinet meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Mr. Krajisnik. What happened from the 12th of May onwards, what happened about the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this before. Before the 12th of May, we needed some representative group, it was called the National Security Council, with Mr. Karadzic as chairman. The moment the government was appointed, that whole previous thing was forgotten. The name disappeared. It did not occur through some sort of officially declared change; it was simply forgotten. This National Security Council, it was just a name. It was -- it never really existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, we have minutes of a joint session of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 14th of May, 1992. That's the way it's described. I've got the ERN number at the moment. That's 01245313. That's described as a joint session of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic. Do you have any comment on that description of that session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By inertia, by force of habit, the person who kept records put this title on these minutes, too. You can look at the previous minutes of all the meetings of the government's National Security Council; they were signed by Mr. Karadzic. However, this one was only signed by Mr. Djeric because it was a cabinet meeting. It was not a session of the government plus council. You can look at the original. I remember that well. It was the last reference to that council. Later on, it was called, simply, cabinet sessions, cabinet meetings. If you have the original you can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would you please guide us to the exhibit number of that 14th of May meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to do, Your Honour. I'm afraid I'm seeking the guidance myself in order to pass on that guidance to the Trial Chamber. So, the answer is: Yes, absolutely, as soon as I'm able to do such a thing I will, but I can't right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Krajisnik, around this time were you personally involved in talks relating to Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't participate. I wasn't involved in any way in talks about the airport, and you can see precisely from those minutes that the government had an interest and appointed some representatives, but that passed me by completely. I had nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour and counsel, the minutes of the joint session of the NSC and the government on 14 May, P583, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm afraid I was only able to go as far as P583, so that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you, Mr. Krajisnik, involved in any continuing talks at that time relating to barracks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that can be called talks, I can say in which way I was involved. I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There came from Belgrade General Boskovic, and I happened to be at Pale, whereas both Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic were absent. Mr. Djeric was at Mount Jahorina. I don't remember whether Mrs. Plavsic was there or not, but she attended one other, different meeting. So he came to us for a meeting, and he explained to us what it was all about. And we started a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was just between us. He told me about the purpose of his visit and I discussed various subjects with him. Later he went to Lukavica; he probably met with Mladic. He went to the Muslim side, led that entire operation, et cetera. Another conversation regarding the barracks, if we can call it that, was at the time when late General Panic, who was the chief of the General Staff, came for a visit. Again, when he came to us, only Mrs. Plavsic and I were there. There was an outright quarrel between Mrs. Plavsic and General Panic because he wanted an apology from her because she had called the Yugoslav People's Army a communist army instead of the Serb army. And she insisted that she was right in calling the army that. He explained that they intended, indeed, to hand over some weapons in order to save their recruits, their conscripts. And it was difficult to get these weapons from Serbia and to ensure safe passage. We could not help with that. They brought in those weapons - I don't know how many - and they handed them over to the Muslim side just outside the UNPROFOR headquarters. We didn't know about it. One protected witness testified here that we learned about it only later. This protected witness was, himself, a military man and he was in the know. That was the contact I had with the military, but I wasn't involved directly, either with the barracks business or the airport talks. Maybe I voiced my opinion, my personal opinion, the opinion of Momcilo Krajisnik, not the holder of any position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, around this time, the middle of May, were you aware of any question of aid being given to the Novo Sarajevo and Hadzici Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean -- do you mean the assistance given by the government to Crisis Staff, aid?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that and I wasn't even supposed to know anything about it because I believe the government assisted Crisis Staffs on its own initiative, because the Crisis Staff were in a very difficult situation. Nobody informed me or kept me posted about it because they were not supposed to. It was a normal thing for the government to do, but I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of talks with the Serbian government around this time, mid-May or the second half of May, involving a Serbian or Republika Srpska delegation of Mr. Djeric, Mr. Pejic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Milojevic, Mr. Markovic, and Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say anything precise about this. It must have been my wish, my intention, to establish contact between the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on one hand, and Serbia on the other hand. That much is certain. At various meetings we expressed the official conclusion that that was necessary. After they left, I don't know whether anything real had been done about it. It's possible that it was decided to establish that contact with the government of Serbia, and I knew about that intention, that plan, to achieve that because we needed that cooperation. The only outside country, the only partner outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was accessible to us, available to us for economic, cultural, and other contacts was Serbia. That's why we needed that contact. When I say "outside country or foreign country," I mean under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But are you saying you do or you don't specifically know about such a delegation meeting representatives of the government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about one meeting that Mr. Ostojic had; however, I don't remember that this meeting was held. But I am inclined to believe that it was held because that intention to establish the contact was real. However, I wasn't aware of the meeting and I don't know what they decided there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, around this same time, middle of May, second half of May 1992, were you aware of there being any issues as to jurisdiction between the main command of the -- main military command of the Serb republic, on the one hand, and the Ministry of the Interior, on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I am going to be precise, but I hope that my answer will be satisfactory. From the outset, there was an overlap between jurisdictions and also a certain degree of rivalry between the armed people or the Territorial Defence on one hand and the Ministry of the Interior. Because the MUP was no longer peacetime police, it was militarised force. They were engaging in other activities apart from maintenance of law and order. And it's very possible that, even back at that time, there was a debate about what was supposed to do what. Those two armed forces were not acting in sync. If you remember that conclusion entrusting Mr. Karadzic's president of the National Security Council to coordinate between the police and the Territorial Defence, he couldn't be entrusted with the coordination with the army because the army at the time was the JNA. So there was a problem, not because they didn't get along well, but because they had their differences on the ground, differences that had to be resolved. And there was, again, a degree of rivalry, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you become personally involved in the -- that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't, but it is possible some sort of consultative meeting was held where those two sides attended, presenting their respective problems before us as if we were some arbitration body. It's like chairing a meeting where two sides point fingers at each other. It's difficult to resolve such differences or even to say who is supposed to implement some sort of synchronisation. It's possible that I attended some meeting of that kind in that role. I once went on a peace-making mission, so to speak, in Sokolac, a mission of that kind, but I didn't attend this meeting. Mr. Tupajic mentioned this Sokolac thing, so I just remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I want us now to look at the government minutes of the 23rd of May, 1992, and that is P529, tab 107?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The ERN there, Your Honour, is 01245320.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I apologise, we haven't yet got the -- the copy of that in your own language, but I'll indicate to you specifically -- well -- the good news --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The good news is that we do, Mr. Krajisnik, behind me coming through to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have copies at this point either, so we'd appreciate it from the Defence or, at a minimum, having it placed on the ELMO in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, don't have copies of what, the B/C/S or the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you would like the English on the ELMO I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- and Mr. Krajisnik to use the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the only way at this point we're going to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems right to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got it, Mr. Krajisnik, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have it in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... still not being on the ELMO -- oh, I see it's in computer evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, now you've said you were not at these meetings, but I want to ask you about number 3 under the list of numbered items. It says: "It was agreed" -- this is the government. "It was agreed that the possibilities and" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The English says "opportunities," Your Honour, but we have some doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can you read the first sentence of number 3, just read it out so the interpreters can tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was agreed to look into the possibilities and the opportuneness of a proclamation of a state of war in municipalities affected by the war. Placed in charge: The Ministry of Defence with consultations with the government vice-president."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Vice-premiere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The sense of opportuneness is rather different from opportunities. Your Honour, we're near enough -- no disrespect to the interpreters digging it off the cuff, we're near enough happy with that for working purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what -- were you involved at this time in any consideration of a question of declaring a state of war, either in municipalities or, more generally, for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, no; but in general terms, yes. And if I might be allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, that's what I invite you to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May in his presentation, Mr. Mladic said that a state of war should be declared as soon as possible. He said that at the Assembly, and this was looking at it from a positive aspect. Later on, since we weren't clear on what the introduction of a state of war or the declaration of a state of war would mean, we discussed this, most probably at some sort of informal meeting, and came to realise that in the soldiers' opinion this would mean the introduction of military rule, administration. And then, as we weren't quite sure, the government took it upon itself to investigate the issue, because we were informed that on the Muslim side preparations were underway for the introduction of a state of war. So that's how I remember it. If I can put it this way, after this realisation - although this wasn't official in any way - but anyway, I was against the introduction of a state of war, I personally, although it wasn't up to me to decide. I was against it because I considered that we should not abolish all the legal organs of government, the Assembly, the government, and so on, and leave it up to the army, which would dominate and have just one body which was supposed to be a sort of collective body which would have a similar term to the Muslim name, the existing Presidency which would be expanded and extended to include a certain number of people, including the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, can you explain the reference here in this item 3 to the possibility of declaring a state of war apparently only in specific municipalities affected by the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a trick of those who advocated the introduction of a state of war. On the whole of the territory of Republika Srpska certain municipalities weren't engulfed by war in the literal sense, but people did leave the territory, they were mobilised, they went up to the front line. So there was this immediate danger of war all over the territory of the Republika Srpska, although in formal terms the decision would be taken just for the decision of the war-engulfed municipalities. But it was quite clear that an immediate threat of war, which held through for the whole territory, would be transformed into a war situation in the legal sense. So you had to see which municipality was concerned, but that was the intention and I remember it well when it was on the agenda for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what was your understanding of how that would work in the legal sense and what the legal effects would be of a declaration of a state of war only in some municipalities but not throughout the whole territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that it had been stated that the regime would change at the level of - how shall I put this? - of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There would be no Assembly, no government, and so on and so forth. Now, those who advocated that, who were in favour of that, would override the people who said: Well, there are lots of municipalities where legal organs can still function. So then they said: Well, all right, let's say this would just be the municipalities taken over by war, but that wasn't feasible. It wasn't feasible for you to introduce into one municipality something that you didn't introduce into another when they were neighbouring municipalities, although partial states of war were declared in certain parts, in the western part, for example. But legislation changed and adapt itself to the war. But at this point in time, nobody knew what this meant, the introduction of a state of war, except that we heard that all the organs should be abolished in favour of just having one body, one organ, just like in 1941 when you had the Partisans, for instance, where the army had the final say. There was the court-martial, that was very worrying. To have a situation as we had it during World War II. If somebody did something wrong, five men would get together, guilty, not guilty, summary execution. So this was analogous to what happened during World War II, and that was the sort of model of the state of war as people saw it. So there were many arguments against it because we didn't want to have this division and general melee.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did any declaration of war only in certain municipalities ever happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995 I think it was, towards the end of the war, towards the end of the conflict, prior to the signing of the Dayton Agreement itself, a large number of municipalities in the western part of the republic was lost. The regular Croatian army helped the Muslim side, assisted the Muslim side and the Croatian side in Bosnia, and almost half the western section was lost. And then the army or, rather, the military leadership exerted strong pressure in favour of introducing a state of war. Then the lawyers got together and they said: Well, it will only apply to that area. That lasted for a very brief period, perhaps just two or three months, but please believe me when I say it had absolutely to effect at all and it wasn't the way we thought in 1990 that it would be by the introduction of court-martials or things like that. But by 1992 nothing of that was introduced, nor was a state of war proclaimed. Now, if we forget a piece of information that we heard about here about SAO Birac who said, quite irresponsibly, that a state of war was being introduced, that is an example that has nothing to do with the actual state of affairs. There were, for example, municipalities who would decide for themselves and say: There will be a state of war here, but that had nothing to do with the legal aspect of the matter and what I'm saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, so you indicated Mr. Mladic had contended for a state of war. Did Mr. Mladic remain thereafter consistently in favour of a declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't that that was so, that he did. The military leadership, when there were -- when there was failure in a certain area, then people would say: Now, had we introduced a state of war, it would have been better, it would have been easier. No, I can't say that he insisted on this. No. It was a suitable justification for failure and when they would be criticised. So that would be to the best of my recollection how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So was Mr. Mladic's position then that he -- he did -- he didn't persist in seeking a declaration of a state of war or that he at any point actually changed his mind and was against that course?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic -- or rather, General Mladic, just like the rest of us, although he was a soldier -- well, this was his first war, although he was a soldier. And what he said at that Assembly meeting, and I'm convinced that at the time he spoke as a soldier, as a military man who'd read about it in some textbooks, that is to say if there was a conflict then a state of war should be declared. I'm sure this is something he had read in a textbook, not having experienced it first-handed. So I can't say that he gave up on the idea, but I can't say that he insisted on it either. Quite simply, this idea to introduce a state of war was something that just the military leadership and General Mladic discussed as a chance not taken, as an opportunity not taken, if they were later criticised, if the army was later criticised. So this was a form of justification. Although, to be quite frank, they did not insist on it, they did not insist that a state of war be declared and introduced right up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- what was Dr. Karadzic's attitude towards the proposal from the military of a declaration of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic at that time was absolutely opposed to this kind of explanation in favour of a state of war, as I've described it, having a court-martial, abolishing civilian organs and so on. He demanded that civilian organs, the civilian authorities still be functional because that is legal and legitimate. He always said there would be a junta of some kind if that were not the case. But if I might be allowed to explain why the constitutional law was passed.
