It was because at one point in time he signed this constitutional law and provision and I can explain why he did so because I learnt this later on, and it has to do with this question of an introduction of a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to invite you just to leave that on one side for the moment and specific aspects of war --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my intention, but, yes, fine, I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, such discussions as there were then between the -- the -- Mr. Mladic and his military colleagues and the civilian leadership, in what sort of meeting did those discussions take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that very rarely Mr. Mladic would come by very rarely without previously giving notice, and then we would sit down and talk about a problem. I don't ever remember Mr. Karadzic calling a meeting at that time and then inviting us to consult each other over a given issue, because the Main Staff was from Pale going to Han Pijesak at a distance of some 40 to 50 kilometres. And we only had telephone communications. So they might have had a telephone communication, a military communications line, or perhaps they contacted each other personally, but yes, there were these ad hoc meetings that he happened to be there and then we discussed issues of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, we have -- we have a minute of the -- that we looked at a little while ago, the first constitutive session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic on the 12th of May, and the next minute we have - we haven't got there yet - is the 31st of May, which is described as the 2nd Session. In between those two minuted meetings, so that's 19 days, can you say how frequently the three members of the Presidency, Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, and Professor Plavsic were meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to be as precise as possible, and probably the right answer would be for me to say I don't know. But what I can tell you is this: That they had various personal contacts. I don't think they had any official meeting or formal Presidency meeting. They would run into each other, then they would sit down, consult each other, and then each go their own way, about their own business. They were preoccupied and taken up with visits by the international representatives, representatives of humanitarian organisations, UNPROFOR. They were inundated with all this, contacts with journalists and others. So their day was very full, but nonetheless they found the time to talk to each other. So I do believe we would sit down for a cup of coffee and discuss certain matters, but I'm not quite sure. Perhaps while we were on the way to somewhere or someone was travelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on the 29th of May, 1992, there was a government meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P65, tab 140. It's in other places as well. It's also in P64A and P583. But specifically P65, tab 140, and the ERN is 01245327.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think we have a copy of that in your own language for you, Mr. Krajisnik. And -- but I can tell you what the point is, Mr. Krajisnik, while we're waiting for that. It -- it was concluded or decided that Mr. Milan Trbojevic -- and this is on page 3 of the English version of that. "Milan Trbojevic and Velibor Ostojic were responsible for visits to the municipalities of Vogosca and Ilijas while Nedeljko Lajic and Ljubomir Zupovic were responsible for the visits to the municipalities of Stari Grad and Centar." It continues: "In the course of these visits they should talk to the Crisis Staffs, take note of the situation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same issue with respect to any government sessions referred to during this session of -- of today's proceeding. We'll try to retrieve everything at the break, but we weren't notified before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry you weren't notified before. I certainly thought you had been, but -- apologies to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not a problem, just wanted to let you know about the logistical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Cooperation is appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I hadn't quite finished. "Take note of the situation. By all means visit the front, make contact with the soldiers, and prepare a report about it for the government." Mr. Krajisnik, were --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, excuse me. For the benefit of the usher, it's page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware of such visits being made, as there noted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. This is something that the government did independently. I don't know whether they were there or not, but if I might be of assistance, the government did what it could. And charted its line of work. It had difficulties, and probably this was one of the tasks, to visit the municipalities around Sarajevo, to receive information from the Crisis Staffs as to what the situation was like, and of course a priority was to see the front line, to see what the situation was like there. Because of course everybody was most interested in that, in Republika Srpska generally and, of course, particularly the government to know what the situation was like up at the front, whether the other side could break through the front and things like that. So these were all topics that were normal, topical, logical. Here we see the government trying to find its own way of work, and I can see that on the basis of certain things and decisions made here in addition to the ones you've already quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Krajisnik, at this time or anywhere around this time, yourself, engage in any such visit to any municipality where you talked to Crisis Staffs, took note of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't within my purview, remit. If I was somewhere - and I don't believe that I was - but that could only have been in my own municipality, in my own home. I might have been there, or if someone were to invite me to go somewhere. But to say that I toured the terrain to establish what the situation was like in the sense it is put here, I never did that. I never had that function, nor did I do anything like that because I had other work to attend to, other preoccupations, and not enough time for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At this time - and to be specific let's take it to the end of May 1992, since the war began - had you, leaving aside Sarajevo, but had you visited the front anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I tend to be rather fearful. I was in Pale. I had my own personal problems, and I was occupied with my own work. There was an Assembly session that was held. There was a lot of work to do, a lot to get through, decisions to implement, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you visited the front anywhere within the Sarajevo region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except if I happened to pass by on my way home, but that was deep into the territory, taking the route that the prisoners took. We didn't see that, but I might have passed within -- or rather, I had to travel a distance of 100 kilometres to arrive home, but the front line wasn't there so I couldn't see the front on my way home. And that came under the competency and authority of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you referred just a moment ago to being occupied with your own work. Well, the position was this, Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't it -- well, first of all it's not alleged before the end of May you were a member of the Presidency. It's common ground that there were only three members of the Presidency at this point. You've given evidence about what happened to the National Security Council or didn't happen at this point in May. You've confirmed - and we see on all the documents - you were not a member of the government. Were you at this time in May a member of any formal group or body within the structure of the Serb Republic or the SDS that was actually meeting at this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was stated here, the SDS froze its work but not pursuant to a decision but in actual fact. It froze its functioning or work. And there was no meeting of the Main Board of the SDS, that is to say I didn't take part in any of that kind of business. Now, what did I do? What came within my competency? I had two basic duties and a third auxiliary duty. Of course that third duty did not take up any less of my time. The first was to deal with Assembly-related matters because the Assembly had become, in a way, a public forum for the ventilation of problems. So it was a sort of forum, although I don't like the word. But you had to prepare material for the meeting and then discussions and debates would be held on them. Up until this date, that is to say from the 12th of May to the 29th of May or, rather, until the end of July, the meeting -- Assembly was not in session. It didn't hold any meetings. Why? I've already explained this. First of all, the corridor was cut across, and from -- you couldn't get from the west to the east; and second, because there were a lot of activities over this other business, that is to say to prepare, analyse, and hold meetings in order to continue the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think we had two or three meetings inclusive with July, and I remember that in July we went to London twice. I think we went twice; we certainly went once to attend the London Conference. And before that there were many meetings as well, consultations on the ground in order to become better acquainted with the terrain, a better acquaintance of the maps and so on. And then later on there was a third, auxiliary duty, if I can put it that way, and I was in Pale mostly, I spent most of my time in Pale for my own problems, but other people including Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Djeric, who had already left to go to Jahorina, I was sort of somebody on duty, a duty officer. When an international representative happened to stop by unannounced, then somebody would receive them, and that person would be me, and talk to them. So I cannot describe all my activities. All I know is that I worked from morning till dusk, from early morning till late at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Your Honour, would it be helpful if I would just -- it would take 30 seconds to reel off the dates of the government and Presidency sessions that I'm going to refer to over the foreseeable future. Your Honour, so far as the government sessions are concerned, I am proposing to look at the 31st May, 1st June, 7th June, 15th and 16th June, 19th June -- well, 26th and 30th possibly, so I'll add them for completeness. And as far as the Presidency -- we won't be dwelling for very long on these items, Your Honour. So far as the Presidency minutes are concerned, 31st May, 8th, 9th, 10th, 13th, 16th, 17th, 25th, and 27th of June. So not 21st and 24th of June, certainly as things stand. Your Honour, we're going to do our best to sort out all this paper. I should say for my team, Your Honour, they are hampered by the fact that there hasn't been a working photocopier in our part of the building all morning, Your Honour, which is torture for them, but we do do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. At the same time, Mr. Stewart, I would like to say a few words and I'm also addressing Mr. Krajisnik. Of course, the Chamber sees at what speed we are progressing at this moment. I don't know where you would put the emphasis. At the same time, the Chamber notices where you ask, for example, Mr. Krajisnik where he was when -- take your last question as an example about whether he -- he was at that time, in May, a member of any formal group or body in the structure of the Serb Republic that was actually meeting at this time, which is a relatively short question, then we get a minutes'-long explanation, not only on what meetings were not held anymore but also why, and in quite some detail. It consumes major portions of time. Certainly it's not direct in the question, but if you -- if you let it go this way and if you think it's all very important to hear all these details of why and if you think it important also to know that some matters that have explained already quite a couple of times to us, I mean Assembly meetings with the corridor is an issue well-known to us, then of course we will let you go without any problem. But of course this Chamber would like to hear as much evidence as could probably be fit in into the time allotted to the Defence. And as I said before, we'll come back to that, if not today, then not later than Monday. We'll adjourn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say on that single last point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I note Your Honour's comments and I would take them on birthday and consider them at all times. As far as the timing is concerned, I'm sure Your Honours can see that knowing how much time Your Honours are suggesting we have had and have left before the weekend is going to be of tremendously greater value than not knowing until after the weekend, if there is any possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give it a try whether we can resolve the matter today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like us to look now, please, at the minutes of the -- what was described as minutes of the session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of the 31st of May, 1992. And that's P64A, binder 25, tab 693, or paper 65, binder 12, tab 142, ERN 00837976. And -- it's all right. Mr. Krajisnik's got it. We've got some spares of the B/C/S there. Mr. Krajisnik, do you see this pretty short minute? 2nd Session of the Presidency of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was held. It was attended by members of the Presidency, Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, and Dr. Koljevic, and the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Momcilo Krajisnik, chaired by Dr. Karadzic. "Current issues regarding the situation in Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were discussed. "After the discussion, the Presidency adopted the decision on the establishment of War Presidencies in municipalities during war or an imminent threat of war." Mr. Krajisnik, do you -- do you remember whether there was such a meeting with just those people who were named present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were present, but there were other people, too, although they had not been named here. I cannot remember all of them, but we never met just the four of us -- I mean, at least not at this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was Mr. Djeric, he's not recorded as being at this meeting. Is that correct, that he was not at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric wasn't there, but somebody from the government was probably there to give the rationale for this decision that we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the decision you're talking about, decision on establishment of War Presidencies --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Krajisnik could have P529, binder 3, tab 110. The ERN is -- if I've got the right number 00509977.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's -- if you could cast your eye over that, that's -- it's dated at the end 31st of May, 1992. On the face of it: Published in the Official Gazette on the 8th of June, 1992, decision on the formation of War Presidencies in municipalities in times of war or the immediate threat of war, that's the decision, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on it being headed "decision on the formation of War Presidencies in municipalities in times of war or the immediate threat of war"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this consultative meeting we only discussed the probably for introducing Presidencies in municipalities. It's for how it was worded later, I believe expert services of the government dealt with that later. This decision wasn't taken at this meeting; we just deliberated on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So where it says in the minute of the meeting: "The Presidency adopted the decision on the establishment of War Presidencies," is it correct to say the Presidency did adopt the decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that at this 2nd Session they expressed their views and adopted the decision. I cannot say so many years later because Mr. Karadzic, after all, signed this decision. I mean, that meeting of the 31st of May which is named the 2nd Session. I was present as a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you understand -- who did you understand to constitute the Presidency at this meeting -- well, I'll stop the question there. Who did you understand to constitute the Presidency at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody in the republic, and certainly I understood that the three members of the Presidency were Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic, and that was the same Presidency that met on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you be given another document, Mr. Krajisnik, which is P64A, binder 23, tab 636, but keep the one, please, that you've got also for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this -- Your Honour, this is the Official Gazette of the Serb People. It's 00448095.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this is apparently an entry in the Official Gazette Monday, 1st June, 1992; however, at the end of the document it purports to be signed by Mr. Karadzic as president of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and dated the 2nd of June, 1992. First of all, are you able to cast any light on the fact that it appears to have been -- on its face, to have been published in the Official Gazette the day before it was actually proclaimed or -- I beg your pardon, perhaps I should avoid the word "proclaimed." The date corresponding with the signature, the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was on the 29th or the 31st of May, but I think it was the 31st that the government passed two enactments. One was the draft law amending the constitutional law about the implementation of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the other was the decision to introduce Presidency -- Presidencies in municipalities in case of war. The session of the government of the 31st of May passed only the decision about Presidencies in municipalities, not this constitutional law. This draft law was brought to Mr. Karadzic and the Presidency directly by somebody from the government. It was signed and sent directly to be published. That was the procedure. I didn't know about this law, and there was no session of the Presidency on the 1st of June. You can verify this. It was just stated that it had been discussed at a session. It must be some sort of mistake. It must have been promulgated on the 1st and enacted on the 2nd. There was no session of the Presidency of the 1st of June; instead, Mr. Karadzic just signed the enactment brought to him by the government. I didn't even know about that enactment. I learnt about it later at an Assembly session that was submitted in the meantime by the Presidency. I didn't even know if there was a session or not. I learned only later that there had been no session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, hold on to the documents you've got, please, but could you be given the minutes of the government meeting of the 31st of May, 1992. That's P583, tab 13. It's also in P65, if I -- I don't have the detailed reference there. So P583, tab 13, and the ERN is 01245335.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here before yes, it is the 17th Session of the cabinet held on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, one thing we did note is there seems to be a discrepancy between the English numbering and the numbering in the original that -- I think the original goes 11B2, instead of number three, law on national defence in the original, it's number 2, and so on. Probably nothing will turn on it, Your Honour, but just to note there in case anyone is ever looking at any time there is that discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the -- Mr. Krajisnik, after the listings of the items 1 to 16, and so on, it carries on with a heading, "1. The proposal of the law on amendments on constitutional law on application of constitution of Serbian Republic of BiH has been accepted in its proposed form." And then the next paragraph: "The proposal of the decisions to form War Presidencies in municipalities during the immediate threat of war or the state of war has been approved provide that," and so on. And I won't go into all the detail. Mr. Krajisnik, so far as you're aware, those are the very same items that we looked at a moment ago, those other two items, decision of formation of War Presidencies and the amendment to constitutional law. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the item -- the law -- the one with that -- those dates, the 1st of June at the top and 2nd of June at the bottom. So let's look back at that one, the law on amending the constitutional law for implementing the constitution. Article 1, and the constitutional law for implementing the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then the Official Gazette references are given, "is amended in article 5 with a new para-3 and reads: 'During a state of war the Presidency is expanded with the following members, the President of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of the Government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" And then there's a renumbering of further paragraphs and then a further paragraph is added or 6 and 7 are added. "'During a state of war the Presidency may decide to establish War Presidencies in the municipalities.'" Mr. Krajisnik, are you able to offer any explanation as to how there came to be, at the very beginning of June, a decision on the formation of War Presidencies when it was apparently only permitted during a state of war and there had not been a state of war declared?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this was done between the Presidency and the government, or maybe just one member of the Presidency and I'll mention another enactment that was adopted in this connection. Because if you remember, perhaps an hour ago we saw that the government assumed the task to investigate the necessity to introduce the state of war, and it adopted this enactment as a contingency in case a state of war is introduced, that they have something to fall back on. But you see from this that the constitutional law that existed was an amendment supplement to the constitution that -- to the effect that two members of the Presidency should perform the functions of president. And this is an amendment that says: During a state of war, the Presidency can be expanded. And it says: "During a state of war the Presidency may form these Presidencies across municipalities." And this decision that was submitted to the Presidency on the 31st states that Presidencies shall be formed, both in case of the immediate threat of war and in a state of war. That's a decision that has no foundation in this amendment of the constitutional law. It was completely wrong in the way it was formulated. This expansion of the Presidency was not something that was supposed to be done in case of an immediate threat of war, only the state of war. But doing this, they must have been assuming, they must have been thinking, that they were going to introduce the state of war; however, that didn't occur and those Presidencies were abolished very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- when you were attending this meeting on the 31st of May, 1992, the session of the Presidency, did anybody give you any indication that you had become a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was impossible. Nobody could have done that nor would I have ever accepted that without being notified at an official Assembly session or through the Official Gazette. I'll give you an example from the Assembly session of the 25th or the 27th of July, 1992, where it was declared, expressly, who was a member of the Presidency. So I was not a member of the Presidency nor did I know that I was a member of the Presidency, nor did anyone, including Mr. Djeric, ever imply that I was a member of the Presidency. You see that last meeting when Mr. Djeric says that he wants to consult with the Presidency and the president of the Assembly? It cannot be the case that everybody except me knew that I was a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like you to be given, please, the minutes of the government meeting of the 1st of June, 1992, which is P64A, tab 676, ERN 01245339. Do you have that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is described as 18th Session and it says -- after the five numbered items then it says: "The minutes of the government meeting held on the 31st of May, 1992, has been accepted without any objections." And then: "1. The government president," and that's Mr. Djeric," has informed government members about the talks that took place at the joint meeting of Serbian Republic of BiH Presidency, Serbian Republic of BiH National Assembly chairman, Serbian Republic government president," Mr. Djeric again, "and Serbian Republic of BiH army Main Staff commander." That, by this time, was Mr. Mladic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When -- can you say when had that joint meeting taken place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that Mr. Mladic was wont to visit without prior notice, very suddenly, and this was one of the consultative meetings that was held without any record kept, and that's what Mr. Djeric refers to. And it's probably at one of those meetings that Mr. Djeric presented certain things, we discussed it, and subsequently he notifies all that to the government. And it's very likely that between the time he said that he needed to meet -- it's very likely that this is -- this happened sometime between the point he said he needed to consult with the Presidency and the speaker of the National Assembly and the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the -- we know, Mr. Krajisnik, there were two government meetings, 31st of May, and 1st of June, so on, on successive days. Mr. Djeric had not reported this item at the meeting the day before; he was reporting it here on the 1st of June. Can you say whether there was such a meeting after the Presidency session which had been held on the 31st of May at which you were present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to say, Mr. Djeric didn't attend the Presidency meeting on the 31st. He wasn't at the Presidency meeting. Possibly in the intervening period -- well, perhaps on the 31st he might have attended a government meeting, I assume. You could have two meetings on the same day, for instance, precisely because the meeting wasn't scheduled. Mladic was there, Mr. Djeric came by or the other way around, and that's how it came about because he needed to meet with the Presidency members and president of the Assembly, and Mr. Mladic happened to be there as well. He couldn't have been invited, but he probably just happened to be there or was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you be given the minutes of the 3rd Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic held on the 8th of June, 1992. That's P64A, bundle 25, tab 685 or P65, bundle 12, tab 152, ERN 00837975. The session commenced at 0900 hours. Present: Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Dr. Djeric. A report on the situation in areas and adoption -- item 1: "The Presidency was briefed on the situation at the front and made a plan of daily activities." Mr. Krajisnik, who briefed the Presidency on the situation at the front?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were able to see here at one of the government meetings that we looked at that there was a piece of information on the ground. We can go back and have a look at that, and it could only have been Mr. Djeric informing or, perhaps, a member of the government might have been there who wasn't recorded here. He -- they might have informed about what happened or was going on, on the ground. Or one more caveat, Mr. Karadzic, for instance, might have contacted Mr. Mladic and simply conveyed to him what he knew. I cannot say exactly which of these provided the information, but that was mostly how information was disseminated from the battle-ground, which was the whole of Republika Srpska after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In your previous answer, Mr. Krajisnik, can we take it that you meant to say that Mr. Mladic might have conveyed to Mr. Karadzic what he knew, rather than the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What I wanted to say is this: It was perhaps Mr. Karadzic who informed -- gave out the information, having received information from Mr. Mladic and possibly from this joint there might have been a piece of information. When Mladic happened to be there, then somebody might have reproduced it with the inclusion of someone in the government. Quite simply, the information could have come from someone in the Main Staff or someone in the government, although these would not have been complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Item 1 records that: The Presidency, having been briefed on the situation, agreed on a plan of daily activities. Was agreement reached at this or any other similar meetings around this time by any taking of a vote?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency never voted by raising one's hands, the ayes and the nays. Mr. Karadzic led the sessions and always tried to have a consensus. I have to be frank and say I never actually considered these meetings to be Presidency sessions. There were the three of them, and I considered that they held consultations and would do their duties. But since it was called this, it was termed that way, that means that after the consultations everyone went about their duties, to implement their assignments, and they would divide up the work. One of them would be in charge of contacts with international representatives, another with humanitarian organisations, and so on and so forth. They had different fields, although as a body they made decisions together. But I never attended a meeting where there would be a voting, all those in favour and all those against, that kind of thing. They went on and within discussing a problem until a consensus had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- did Mr. Djeric ever say anything to you or in your presence which indicated that he regarded himself as a member of an expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Mr. Djeric liked to have things very -- strictly legal, and he said: I want to know what the government does and what the president -- what the job of the Presidency is. And he always insisted that the Presidency record the meetings with minutes, have their rules of procedure, just as I did. But he went even further in doing that. So absolutely, no, he did his job to the best of his ability. He probably had subjective and objective difficulties, people presented problems, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik be given, please, the minutes of the fourth meeting. That's -- that's the 9th of June. It's P64A, bundle 25, tab 723, or P65, bundle 12, tab 155, ERN 00837974.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Krajisnik, this is described as minutes of the fourth expanded meeting of the War Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, considering the minutes of the previous meeting as well, the one we looked at a moment ago, the 8th of June, did you -- did you receive these minutes of these meetings at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we needed something to remind us, an aide-memoire, so that we knew what we had studied after holding consultations of that kind. And I'm quite certain that we didn't have this type of minutes, in this form, set out in this form. I would jot down something, take a note of something that was in -- that I was interested in, but I never saw the minutes set out in this form before I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, this -- there are two differences in that heading to this document, as compared with the previous document and, in fact, the one before as well. It's described as the 4th expanded meeting of the War Presidency, so both the word "expanded" and the word "war" are there when they were not in the heading of the minutes of the previous meeting. Mr. Krajisnik, can you cast any light on either or both of those differences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we can see -- it says: From the 4th expanded meeting. An expanded meeting is considered a meeting when a body whose members are legally elected and when that body -- when you have outside -- people from outside attending, outside collaborators, and here it was Mr. Mladic and Mr. Tolimir, who very rarely attended consultations of this kind. So probably the person who wrote this down thought that the best term to be used was "expanded meeting," because they considered myself and Mr. Djeric to be locals, that is to say people who were seen very often. Now, the concept of a War Presidency, that term is used there because the person who kept these minutes in one way or another wrote down this attribute of War Presidency because soldiers - if I can put it that way - attended, military men, so that we can see that in all the minutes when meetings were being held in a state of imminent war, that was not there. But this is a consultative meeting with the army. So it should not, in my view, be a Presidency meeting, but I can see that that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned co-counsel tells me he needs a couple of minutes to deal with a practical matter arising out of the session earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- there's not much time left, so then we would conclude for the day just --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he needs a couple of minutes now, Your Honour, in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour, I understand there's no problem of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Prosecution will also need a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another hearing at quarter past 2.00, so I'm defending my afternoon time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I quickly hand this map to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I want to do is give a copy of this map to Mr. Krajisnik to take away with him for the weekend and invite him to mark it up with a black pen the route of the bus so that he can explain it on Monday and save time all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if he's aware of the route the bus took.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If he could mark the map up in the way he wanted to earlier in relation to the intercept we dealt with. I've got a copy for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Mr. Krajisnik, you've understood what homework you've got for the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's all I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's even less than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness -- the accused repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need another portion here, more of the map, more of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, make do with that as best you can, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever roads are on the map, please fill them, and then we'll find an itinerary for the missing part. It might not be of greatest importance to fill in the whole of the route. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to address the issue of the pending cross-examination. We have been in direct examination for 18 days. We will be continuing into next week. As we raised earlier with the Court, the 65 ter summary was factually deficient, it was incomplete, and counsel acknowledged that. We have -- it was topical, essentially, in terms of what topics would be addressed. We have been preparing diligently in the course of this exercise to prepare for cross-examination. The Defence had considerable time prior to the direct examination where they could prepare without the -- the distractions of court and the imminence of court. We are in a position when we start our cross-examination we have concluded that we also will need some time, a break, between the end of the direct examination and the cross-examination. We would like at this point to inform the Court that by our best calculation it would be three regularly scheduled court days which we would need to organise the exhibits, organise ourselves to prepare properly for that cross-examination. So that is our request. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. It's another scheduling issue. When the Defence used its time to prepare, they were put in a position where they could choose -- I remember the extra days. We said to the Defence: Do you want to use those further days for further time to present the evidence or for further preparation? So they had to make a choice at the time. How do I have to understand your request to get additional days for preparation which would be deducted from the time of cross or would you want to have them in addition to the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, we were thinking in addition to the time, Your Honour, frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me that that's the answer, Mr. Harmon. We'll consider the matter and of course also together with the still-pending issue, and we'll see whether we could give you an answer. I can't promise that to you. These last weeks, usually the Judges have approximately three meetings during each break, sometimes two, which gives us -- allows us for a cup of coffee now and then. I have my next Status Conference at quarter past 2.00, so therefore time is very limited, and I have not asked for additional time to prepare for that. But we'll see what we can do and to what extent we can give you the decisions you are asking us to give to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I take 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I know counsel have a meeting at 2.15 among themselves as well. Your Honours, we would have, in the usual way, an opportunity, we trust, of making submissions in relation to what are now the connected issues of the question of time for in chief and Mr. Harmon's application made a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll also consider how to deal with this matter. No courtroom has been reserved for this afternoon. Of course a Status Conference takes time to end as well. It might be that further communication might be needed later this afternoon on the matter because it really becomes urgent. Therefore, the parties should keep themselves available for further communication this afternoon, if need be. If so, you'll be contacted by the -- I should say by the Legal Officer, since the Senior Legal Officer is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We shall be at Your Honour's disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn until next Monday. Mr. Registrar, would it be -- in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00, I think it's the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24
